title: Plants Called Mothers
hookLine: the Vedas call the plants mothers, which is why so many Hindu homes water a tulsi every morning
carry: the plants are mothers: why hindus water the tulsi
tomorrow: why do Hindus sip water from the palm before worship?

cards: Brown, white, red, dappled, dark. That's not a paint chart. It's how one Atharva Veda hymn begins its roll call of the plants.
Before it asks them for anything, it looks at them and sorts them by color, the way a kid sorts crayons or a cook lines up vegetables on a cutting board.
An empty lot in summer holds the same crowd: weeds, wildflowers and grasses, many without a name to a passerby. The hymn calls them up one color at a time, and then calls them all.

teach.h: ALL THE PLANTS, CALLED BY COLOR.
teach.b: The Atharva Veda's long hymn to the plants opens, in paraphrase: the brown ones, the white, the red, the dappled, the dark and the black, all the plants, we call on. It asks them to protect the one who is sick.
The Rig Veda has a hymn to the plants too, the oshadhi, plants that heal, and it tells a small scene.
The plants gather and talk together with Soma, their king, and make a promise: whoever the priest tends for healing, O king, we carry across to safety.
And it speaks to them with a startling word: plants, mothers, I speak to you as goddesses. Mothers. Not ingredients.
That's a Hindu teaching you can see from the street. In many Hindu homes, in a courtyard in India or a pot on a New Jersey porch, stands a tulsi, holy basil, honored as a goddess and dear to Vishnu.
Every morning someone waters it, often with a prayer, and many light a small lamp beside it at dusk.

teach.h: THE GREEN WORLD IS ALIVE WITH GOD.
teach.b: The teaching under it: the divine isn't kept in temples only; the green world is alive with it, and you treat it the way you'd treat a mother.
One honest note: these hymns aren't prescriptions, and nothing here says what to take for an illness. They teach how to look. A plant in a pot can be decoration, or it can be family.

how: Many Hindu homes keep a tulsi plant, honored as a goddess and dear to Vishnu, watering it each morning and lighting a lamp beside it at dusk; the Vedic hymns to the plants are kept in recitation, and Ayurvedic tradition later developed its own learning about plants.

games.q: what does “the atharva veda's healing hymns” mean?
o: a book of recipes for cooking with medicinal herbs
Vedic hymns that call on plants and words to help the sick
prayers said only at the very end of someone's life

p: a plant, especially one that heals
what the Rig Veda calls the plants
the plants' king in the hymn

s: a Vedic hymn speaks to the plants as mothers
plants, mothers, I speak to you as goddesses.
in Hindu homes, tulsi is just a kitchen herb
it's honored as a goddess, dear to Vishnu: watered each morning, given a lamp at dusk.
these hymns tell you what to take for an illness
they aren't prescriptions. they teach how to look at plants: as mothers.

games.q: the family tulsi is drooping because everyone's been busy. by today's teaching, what is it?
o: a sacred plant treated like family: water it, with a prayer if you pray
an ingredient to pick before it dies
games.why: the Rig Veda speaks to the plants as mothers, and Hindu homes honor the tulsi as a goddess. you look after a mother.

practice: Find something green: a houseplant, a tree outside the window, herbs on the counter. If there's water near, give it a little, the way many Hindus water the tulsi each morning. If you pray, thank it the way you'd thank a mother.
If you don't, simply name its color as plainly as the hymn does, and think of what it took to grow.

wordCard.voice: The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Today, plants called up by color, spoken to as mothers, and a tulsi watered every morning.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a plant or herb, especially one that heals. The Vedic hymns speak to the plants directly.
